text: About 2,500 years ago, the ancestors of the Taíno came to the Caribbean islands from South America.
The Taíno lived on islands such as Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola and Puerto Rico.
src: DNA studies suggest that the Taíno descended from a wave of pottery-making farmers, the Ceramic Age people, who entered the Caribbean from north-eastern South America about 2,500 years ago
from the Lucayan Archipelago through Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola and Puerto Rico to Guadeloupe

text: They grew cassava, a root crop, in heaped-up mounds of earth.
Women squeezed out its poison and ground it into flour for bread.
src: Cassava (yuca) was planted with a wooden digging tool, the coa, in heaped mounds called conucos, which drained the soil and let roots be stored in the ground
women squeezed the poison out of cassava and ground it into flour for bread

text: Families lived in large round houses around a village square, led by a chief called a cacique.
Their homes held cotton hammocks, and the English word hammock comes from their word hamaca.
src: Most people lived in large round houses, bohíos / built around a central plaza / under a chief known as a cacique

text: They honoured zemís, spirits and ancestors, carved in wood, stone and shell.
In the village square, they celebrated the deeds of their ancestors with songs.
src: Their religion centred on zemís, spirits and ancestors given form in carved wood, stone, shell and cotton
In the areítos held in the plaza the deeds of the ancestors were celebrated / the village sang its epic to maracas

text: They played a ball game called batey, with teams of up to 30 players and a solid rubber ball.
Games may have helped settle quarrels between villages.
src: The Taíno played a ceremonial ball game, batey, with teams of 10 to 30 players and a solid rubber ball
games are believed to have settled disputes between communities

text: After Columbus came, the Spanish forced the Taíno to work, and war and disease killed most of them.
Yet their descendants live on, and thousands of people in Puerto Rico and beyond call themselves Taíno today.
src: Spanish conquest after 1492 brought forced labour, war and epidemics that killed most Taíno within decades
yet Taíno descent, customs and identity survive in the Caribbean today / In the 2010 United States census 9,399 people in Puerto Rico identified as Taíno
